lesson.title: Perception as inference

steps.headline: One sense gives a wobbly reading

lead.text: Start with sight alone. You look at the block and your eyes give you a number, say 50 mm. Look again after blinking and you get 49, and the next look gives 52. The readings gather around the true height, yet no single look is exact. Over many looks they average out near 50 mm and typically stray from that average by about 2 mm.

That typical stray is the standard deviation, or SD, the usual size of a scatter around an average. A small SD means the readings bunch tightly, so one look is nearly as good as any other. A large SD means they are scattered, so any one look could be well off.

Every source of information about the world wobbles in this way and has an SD of its own. Psychologists call such a source a cue. Sight is a cue to the block's height. Touch is another. Because no cue is exact, working out the height is a matter of inference: a best guess drawn from the evidence you have.

Now put on the thick gloves and feel the block. Your fingers say 56 mm. Gloves dull the sense of touch, so these readings wobble more than the ones from your eyes, with an SD of 4 mm against sight's 2 mm.

You are left with two readings, 50 mm and 56 mm, which cannot both be exact. One way out is to split the difference and say 53 mm. That treats the two cues as equally good, and whether they are is the real question.

Think of two friends giving you directions. One has lived in the area for years and the other visited once. If they disagree you would not give them equal say. You would lean towards the friend whose directions have turned out right more often, while still listening to the other. The mind faces the same choice with every pair of senses, and it makes it with a rule that can be written down.
Sight reads the block at 50 mm and its readings wobble by an SD of 2 mm. Touch through the gloves reads 56 mm with an SD of 4 mm. You have to give one best estimate of the height.

steps.headline: Weighing cues by how steady they are

lead.text: The steadier cue should count for more, and there is a precise way to say how much more. Give each cue a number for how far it can be trusted, called its reliability, and set it to 1 ÷ SD², where SD² means the SD multiplied by itself. A cue with an SD of 1 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (1 × 1) = 1. A cue with an SD of 3 mm has a reliability of 1 ÷ (3 × 3) = 1/9. Because the SD is multiplied by itself, a cue that wobbles more loses reliability quickly.

Each cue's weight is its share of the total. Add the reliabilities, then divide each cue's reliability by that total, so that the weights add up to 1. The combined estimate is the weighted average: multiply each reading by its weight and add the results.
The figure shows a second, shorter block. Sight reads 30 mm with an SD of 1 mm, and touch reads 36 mm with an SD of 3 mm. The taller, narrower curve belongs to the steadier cue.

afterFigure.text: The combined estimate, marked in teal, sits close to the sight reading. If both cues were equally steady they would get equal weights, and the estimate would fall exactly halfway between them. The midpoint is a special case, correct only when the cues are matched.

lead.text: Reliability depends on the SD multiplied by itself. Work it out for a cue with an SD of 2 mm, and again for the same cue after its SD has grown to 4 mm.

steps.headline: For a second, shorter block, sight reads 30 mm (SD 1 mm) and touch reads 36 mm (SD 3 mm). Find the combined estimate.

workedSteps.text: Divide each by the total, 1 + 1/9 = 10/9, to get the weights.
Weight the readings and add them.
Read the result: 30.6 mm sits well below the midpoint of 33 mm, close to the steadier cue.

lead.text: Back to the first block. Sight reads 50 mm with an SD of 2 mm. Touch through the gloves reads 56 mm with an SD of 4 mm. Weight each cue by its reliability.

steps.headline: Two cues are sharper than one

lead.text: The combined estimate has a second advantage over each cue taken alone: it wobbles less. Two witnesses who each saw part of an event give a better account together than the better witness gives alone, because each fills in what the other left uncertain.

The SD of the combined estimate follows from the reliabilities. Add the two reliabilities and take the square root of the total. The combined SD is 1 divided by that root. Written out, it is 1 ÷ √(1/SD₁² + 1/SD₂²). Take two cues with SDs of 5 mm and 12 mm. Their reliabilities are 1/25 and 1/144, which add up to 169/3600. The square root of that is 13/60, and 1 divided by 13/60 is 60/13, about 4.6 mm. That is smaller than both 5 and 12.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the narrow teal curve is the combined estimate. It is taller and thinner than either cue's own curve, so using both senses pins the height down more tightly than the better sense could by itself. Even a poor cue helps, as long as its errors are unrelated to the other cue's errors.

lead.text: Two cues give independent readings of the same block. One has an SD of 3 mm and the other an SD of 4 mm. Use the formula for the combined SD.

steps.headline: What you expect is evidence too

lead.text: So far every cue has come through a sense. A third source of evidence needs no sense at all: what you already expect to see. Suppose a line flashes up for an instant and you cannot make out its tilt. If you expect it to be upright, that expectation pulls what you see towards upright.

The mind treats the expectation like one more cue. It has a reading, such as a tilt of 0° for an upright line, and an SD that says how firmly the expectation is held. Expectations built over many years are firm, so their SD is small and they carry a large weight whenever the glimpse is poor. An expectation used this way is called a prior, because it is in place before the new evidence arrives. Perception shaped by what you know and expect, instead of being built only from the incoming signal, is top-down processing.
In the figure, a line is expected to be upright (0°, SD 2°) and the glimpse says 8° (SD 4°).

afterFigure.text: The combined tilt stays close to upright. A hollow mask seen from the inside shows the same thing at a larger scale. Its surface is dented inwards, yet it looks like an ordinary face bulging outwards, because the expectation that faces bulge is so firm that it outweighs the shading that says otherwise.

lead.text: A line flashes up briefly. You expect it to be upright. Your eyes catch it only for an instant and report a tilt.

lesson.orientation: Combine noisy cues and prior expectations by their reliability, as the perceptual system appears to.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A small wooden block sits on the table in front of you. Looking at it, you judge it to be 50 mm tall, but when you put on thick gloves and feel it your fingers say 56 mm. The block has not changed, yet the two senses disagree by 6 mm and you still need one answer.

This is the ordinary state of perception. Neither sense hands you the block's true height. Each gives a report with some wobble in it, and the mind has to decide how far to believe each one before it settles on a single answer.

This lesson follows that one block. It begins with how a single sense gives a wobbly reading, adds a second sense and works out how much to trust each, and shows that two readings together are sharper than either. It ends with what you expect to see, which turns out to count as evidence as well.

intro.promise: By the end you'll combine two readings by how steady each is, and treat an expectation as one more reading.

recap.keyIdea: The mind weighs every cue, expectation included, by its reliability, 1 ÷ SD². The combined estimate leans towards the steadier cue and is sharper than either cue alone.

blocks.text: Back at the block, you weighted sight and touch to get 51.2 mm. You found that cues with SDs of 3 mm and 4 mm combine to an SD of 2.4 mm, below both. You also saw a line glimpsed at 10° appear tilted by only 1°, because the expectation of an upright line carried most of the weight.

recap.nextHook: Perception gives the mind its best guess about what is in front of it. The next lesson asks how much the mind can hold on to afterwards, starting with two lists of nine digits and a ten-second wait.

questions.prompt: Hearing places a voice 10° to the right (SD 8°); vision places the moving lips at 0° (SD 4°). Where is the voice heard, in degrees to the right?
hints: Compute 1/SD² for each sense.
Hearing's weight is its reliability over the total.
Multiply that weight by 10°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1/64 and 1/16 give hearing weight (1/64)/(5/64) = 0.2; location = 0.2 × 10 = 2°. Vision captures the sound, as in ventriloquism.

questions.onCorrect: Hearing is the less reliable sense, so vision pulls the heard location towards the lips. This is the ventriloquist effect.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint. Vision is steadier, so it should count for more.
That gives most of the weight to hearing, the less reliable sense.

questions.prompt: Perception guided by knowledge and expectation, rather than built only from incoming sensory features, is called what kind of processing?
hints: It runs in the opposite direction to bottom-up processing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Top-down processing: knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived.

questions.onCorrect: Knowledge and expectation shape what is perceived. That is top-down, the reverse of building from features.

misconceptions.feedback: Bottom-up builds perception from the incoming features alone. This asks for the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Cue A reads 12 with SD 2. Cue B reads 18 with SD 6. Weighting by 1 ÷ SD², what is the combined estimate?
hints: Find 1 ÷ SD² for each cue.
Each cue's weight is its reliability over the total.
Multiply each reading by its weight and add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1/4 and 1/36 give A a weight of (9/36)/(10/36) = 0.9. Estimate = 0.9 × 12 + 0.1 × 18 = 10.8 + 1.8 = 12.6.

questions.onCorrect: The steadier cue A carries 0.9 of the weight, so the estimate stays close to its reading.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives most of the weight to the less reliable cue.

questions.prompt: Roughly where should your best single estimate of the height land?
hints: Which of the two senses would you trust more here?
Should a trusted cue count for the same as a doubtful one?

acceptedIdeas: Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closer to 50 mm: your eyes are the more reliable cue, so they should count for more.

choices.label: Closer to 56 mm than to 50 mm
Closer to 50 mm than to 56 mm

questions.onCorrect: A steadier cue should count for more. You leaned towards sight before anyone gave you a formula.

misconceptions.feedback: The midpoint treats both cues as equally trustworthy, and they are not.
That follows the gloved fingers, which are the less reliable cue.

questions.prompt: A cue's SD doubles from 2 to 4. By what factor does its reliability, 1 ÷ SD², fall?
hints: Work out 1 ÷ SD² before and after.
The SD is squared before you take one over it.
Compare 1/4 with 1/16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliability falls from 1/4 to 1/16, a factor of 4.

questions.onCorrect: SD is squared, so doubling it cuts reliability to a quarter.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the square. Doubling the SD makes SD² four times as big.
That is the fraction left. The question asks by what factor it falls.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Reliability is one over the variance, 1/SD².
Vision's share is its reliability divided by the sum of both.
Multiply each reading by its share and add.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Weights 1/4 and 1/16 give vision 0.25/0.3125 = 0.8; estimate = 0.8 × 50 + 0.2 × 56 = 51.2 mm.

questions.onCorrect: Weights follow 1 ÷ SD², so the steadier cue counts for more than the midpoint would give it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to touch, but touch is the less reliable cue here.

questions.prompt: Why does the answer land nearer 30 than the midpoint, 33?
hints: Which cue has the smaller SD?

acceptedIdeas: The reading of 30 comes from the steadier cue, so it carries more weight.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The steadier cue has the bigger weight, so the estimate leans towards its reading.

choices.label: The first number always counts for more.
A smaller reading always counts for more.
The reading of 30 comes from the steadier cue, so it carries more weight.

questions.onCorrect: The estimate leans towards the steadier cue's reading, which is the one with the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: Order does not matter. Only the SDs set the weights.
Size of the reading does not matter. Only reliability sets the weight.

questions.prompt: What is the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: The more reliable cue now is touch.
Combine 0.2 of the vision reading with the rest from touch.
questions.onCorrect: Touch is now the steadier cue, so it carries most of the weight and pulls the estimate towards its reading.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain midpoint. The steadier cue should count for more.
That uses the earlier weights. The steadier cue has changed.

questions.prompt: One cue has an SD of 4 mm. A second independent cue has an SD of 6 mm. What is the combined SD like?
hints: Does adding a second cue add information or remove it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adding any independent cue sharpens the estimate, so the combined SD is below both.

questions.onCorrect: Every independent cue adds information, so the combined SD ends up below the smaller SD.

misconceptions.feedback: An average of the two would land there, but combining cues does better than an average.
Combining cues never makes an estimate worse than the best cue alone.

questions.prompt: What is the standard deviation of the combined estimate, in millimetres?
hints: Add the two reliabilities 1/9 and 1/16.
Use the common denominator 144.
Take one over the square root of the sum.
questions.onCorrect: Add the reliabilities, then invert: the combined SD sits below both cues.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the two SDs. Combining cues does better than averaging.
That adds the squares of the SDs and takes the root, which makes a wider spread. The formula adds reliabilities, 1 ÷ SD².

questions.prompt: You expect a line to be upright at 0° (SD 1°). You glimpse it at 10° (SD 3°). Combining expectation and glimpse by reliability, what tilt do you perceive, in degrees?
hints: Treat the expectation as a cue with its own SD.
The expectation's weight is 1/(1 + 1/9).
Only the glimpse's share multiplies a non-zero reading.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Reliabilities 1 and 1/9 give the expectation weight 0.9; perceived tilt = 0.9 × 0 + 0.1 × 10 = 1°.

questions.onCorrect: The steadier expectation carries most of the weight, so what you see is pulled almost to upright.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the midpoint of expectation and glimpse. The steadier one should count for more.
That gives the larger weight to the glimpse, but the expectation is the steadier cue.
